summary: Describes the management architecture for MPLS and how the various MIB modules for MPLS relate to each other. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS has many pieces to monitor. This memo is a map showing how all the different monitoring dictionaries fit together.

subtitle: The map of MIB modules for monitoring and managing MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: MPLS is complex, with many interacting components: routers switching labels, label distribution protocols, traffic engineering tunnels, and interfaces. Operators need a way to monitor and manage all of these through a single management framework.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF has defined a family of MIB modules (managed object collections) for MPLS, each covering one aspect: label switching, label distribution, traffic engineering, FEC-to-NHLFE mapping, and TE links. This RFC documents how these modules fit together and relate to each other.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can now use SNMP to query and configure MPLS systems in a consistent way, understanding which MIB modules cover which parts of the network and how data flows between them.

today: RFC 4221 is Informational and remains the reference architecture for MPLS network management via SNMP and MIB modules. The modules it describes are now mature and widely deployed in MPLS networks.

sections.title: MPLS and SNMP Management
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) forwards packets using short labels instead of long IP addresses, enabling traffic engineering and virtual private networks. Managing an MPLS network means monitoring labels, tracking label paths, measuring traffic, and configuring constraints. The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) is the standard tool for this, and it uses Management Information Base (MIB) modules to define what data can be read or written.

This RFC does not define new MIB modules; instead, it explains how the MPLS MIB modules defined in other RFCs fit together. It describes the OID tree structure, which is the naming hierarchy for all MPLS managed objects, and shows which modules import from which others.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is like a checklist of questions you can ask a network switch. MPLS has many things to monitor, so many RFCs define different checklists for different parts. This memo shows how all those checklists relate.

sections.title: The MPLS MIB Module Family
sections.content:
The MPLS management architecture consists of six core MIB modules organized under a shared OID tree at transmission.mplsStdMIB:

MPLS-TC-STD-MIB defines textual conventions (standard ways of representing data) that all other MPLS MIB modules use. For example, labels are a central concept in MPLS, and this module defines how labels are represented. All other MPLS MIB modules import from it.

MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB is at the heart of MPLS management. It models a Label Switching Router: the basic label-forwarding behavior, the label forwarding information base (LFIB), and the cross-connects that map incoming labels to outgoing labels. All other MIB modules reference this one.

MPLS-LDP-STD-MIB manages the Label Distribution Protocol, which negotiates which labels to use for which packets. Three variants exist for different link types: LDP over ATM, LDP over Frame Relay, and generic LDP.

MPLS-TE-STD-MIB manages MPLS tunnels that are traffic-engineered, meaning they have constraints (bandwidth, latency) and explicit paths.

MPLS-FTN-STD-MIB manages how incoming packets are classified and assigned to a Label Switched Path (LSP) at the ingress of an MPLS domain, using Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs).

TE-LINK-STD-MIB manages TE links, which bundle multiple physical links into a single logical link for traffic engineering.
sections.plainLanguage: Six MIB modules are like six different departments: one for naming, one for basic switching, one for distributing labels, one for engineered tunnels, one for choosing which tunnel to use, and one for bundled links.

sections.title: How the Modules Depend on Each Other
sections.content:
The MPLS MIB modules form a dependency hierarchy. MPLS-TC-STD-MIB sits at the root: all other modules import textual conventions from it. MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB is the core: all other modules (TE, LDP, FTN) reference objects in MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB to identify the underlying LSPs they manage. For example, a tunnel managed in MPLS-TE-STD-MIB points to cross-connect entries in MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB to show which label mappings it uses.

The LDP modules (standard, generic, ATM, Frame Relay) import from MPLS-LDP-STD-MIB, which manages the core LDP protocol. The FTN module uses the LSR module to identify where to send traffic. The TE LINK module uses the Interfaces MIB to represent bundled physical links. The choice of which module to use depends on the task: to monitor basic label switching, query MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB; to manage LDP, add MPLS-LDP-STD-MIB; to engineer traffic, add MPLS-TE-STD-MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic module is like a library catalog that lists every shelf. The other modules reference it to show which shelves they manage. Modules can also reference each other when they deal with the same LSP.

sections.title: Interfaces and LSP Management
sections.content:
MPLS MIB modules integrate with the standard Interfaces MIB to model both physical MPLS-capable interfaces and logical MPLS tunnels. Each MPLS-capable interface gets a unique ifIndex, and tables in MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB (mplsInterfaceTable, mplsInSegmentTable, mplsOutSegmentTable) use this ifIndex to reference incoming and outgoing interfaces for label switching.

MPLS tunnels are also represented as entries in the Interfaces MIB table if the mplsTunnelIsIf object is set to TRUE. A tunnel gets its own ifIndex and ifType of 150 (mpls). This allows a tunnel to be monitored like a physical interface, with operational status and performance counters.

TE links are similar: they are represented as entries in the Interfaces MIB with ifType 200 (teLink). Multiple TE links can be bundled, which creates a stacked interface hierarchy showing which physical links are grouped into which logical TE links.
sections.plainLanguage: Both real hardware links and virtual tunnels are treated as 'interfaces' so the same monitoring tools can watch both. This lets you see what is a real wire and what is a virtual path.

sections.title: Using the MIB Modules to Manage MPLS
sections.content:
All LSPs appear in MPLS-LSR-STD-MIB as cross-connect entries, regardless of how they are created. An LSP established by LDP also appears there; a tunnel created by traffic engineering also appears there. LDP-specific tables (mplsLdpLspTable, mplsFecTable, mplsLdpLspFecTable) add protocol-specific details and can correlate LSPs with FECs.

Traffic-engineered tunnels can be represented in MPLS-TE-STD-MIB with constraints (bandwidth, hop limit, explicit path), and their underlying LSPs appear as cross-connects in the LSR module. The FTN module shows which packets are assigned to which LSP at ingress: for example, packets matching a source/destination address pair and DSCP value are mapped to a specific LSP via an NHLFE (Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry).

LSPs can be created manually (via SNMP SET commands or a CLI) or dynamically (via LDP or traffic engineering signaling). The management modules support all three. Operations like monitoring tunnel status, counting traffic, or changing constraints can all be done via SNMP queries and updates to these MIB tables.
sections.plainLanguage: One master table tracks every label path. Other modules add details: 'This path was set up by LDP' or 'This tunnel has a bandwidth limit of 1 Gbps' or 'These packets go to that tunnel.'

sections.title: MPLS Extensions and Alternatives
sections.content:
Related working groups have produced MIB modules that interact with the core MPLS modules. The PWE3 working group created modules for Pseudo Wire Emulation, which uses MPLS tunnels as the transport. The PPVPN working group defined the PPVPN-MPLS-VPN-STD-MIB to manage MPLS VPNs, including virtual routing and forwarding (VRF) tables. The CCAMP working group developed modules for GMPLS (Generalized MPLS), which extends MPLS to optical and other technologies.

The Traffic Engineering Working Group also produced a minimalistic TE-MIB module separate from the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB. TE-MIB is simpler and focuses on tunnel endpoints (ingress only) without hop-by-hop decomposition. MPLS-TE-STD-MIB is more detailed and integrates tightly with LSR-STD-MIB, allowing decomposition of tunnels into cross-connects. Choose TE-MIB for simplicity or MPLS-TE-STD-MIB for full control and integration.
sections.plainLanguage: Other teams added modules for specific uses: virtual private networks, pseudo wires, optical networks, and simplified tunnel management. Pick the one that fits your use case.
